opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things we've spent the most time on, because for a product like Asimov, which is really about deep code understanding for engineering teams, the generic benchmarks just don't capture what matters. Something like SWE-bench tells you whether a model can patch an isolated bug. It doesn't tell you whether it can answer the kinds of questions a senior engineer at a large company actually asks: "Why was this service designed this way?" "What breaks if I change this interface?" "Who owns this, and what was the reasoning in that design doc from two years ago?"

So the process starts very close to the customer. When we onboard a team, we sit with their engineers and collect the real questions they're asking, the ones that today take hours of digging through code, Slack threads, tickets, and docs. Then we look at where Asimov's answers fall short. Those failures are the most valuable signal we have, because each one points at a capability gap rather than a one-off bug.

From there we turn those failures into evals. We abstract the question type, figure out what a great answer looks like (often with the customer's own engineers grading or writing the reference), and build a set that represents that category. The goal is that the eval isn't tied to one customer's codebase but captures something general, like tracing behavior across many repositories, or reconciling conflicting information between the code and the documentation.

Then it's a pretty tight loop. The evals tell us where to focus, whether that's retrieval, how the agent explores a codebase, or the reasoning itself, and when we improve we check that it generalizes and doesn't just overfit to the cases we saw. In the RL world I came from, the reward signal is everything. Here the customer, in a sense, defines the reward. Our job is to turn their messy, real-world needs into something measurable enough that we can actually optimize against it.

r001.rationale: The response describes collecting real customer questions, but does not frame this as the AI-era counterpart of startup customer discovery.

r002.rationale: It starts from customer questions and answer failures, identifies capability gaps, and turns those into evaluations that guide work on retrieval, agent exploration, and reasoning.

r003.rationale: The response does not say product changes are restricted to features and agent design or that improvement therefore depends on third-party model capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about constantly, because the honest answer is that most of the public benchmarks don't tell you very much about whether an agent is actually useful inside a real engineering organization. SWE-bench is a good example. It's a reasonable proxy for "can a model fix a well-specified bug in an open-source Python repo," but that's a tiny slice of what engineers actually do all day. Most of the work is understanding a codebase you didn't write, figuring out why some system is behaving a certain way, tracking down context that lives in Slack threads or design docs or in somebody's head. So if you optimize purely for the public leaderboards, you end up with something that looks great on paper and then falls over the moment you drop it into a real company.

So the way we approach it is we start from the customer. When we deploy Asimov with a team, we spend a lot of time just watching how engineers actually interact with it. What questions are they asking? Where does it give a confident answer that turns out to be wrong? Where does it say "I don't know" when the information was actually there in the codebase? And then we try to turn those failure modes into evaluations. Not abstract ones, but things that look like the real distribution of work.

One concrete example is codebase understanding. A new engineer joins a team and asks, "how does the authentication flow work in this service?" That's a question where the answer is spread across many files, maybe some infrastructure config, maybe a PR description from two years ago. We built evals around exactly that kind of question, where there's a verifiable ground truth, often validated by the engineers who actually own that code, and we can measure whether the agent gets it right and whether it's citing the right sources. That turned out to be much more predictive of whether a team found Asimov valuable than any of the coding benchmarks.

The other thing I'd say is that the evals have to be grounded in verification, because that's really the whole lesson from reinforcement learning. If you have a clear reward signal, you can improve against it. So we try to design the evals so that correctness is something we can actually check, rather than vibes. And then we close the loop. The customer feedback shapes the eval, the eval shapes the training and the system design, and then we go back to the customer and see if the thing that was broken is actually fixed. It's less glamorous than chasing a leaderboard, but it's the thing that actually moves the product.

r001.rationale: The response says the team starts from customers and observes engineers, but does not frame this as the AI-era counterpart of startup customer discovery.

r002.rationale: It describes turning customer questions and observed failure modes into evaluations, then using those evaluations to shape training and system design.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe limiting changes to product features and agent design or explain dependence on third-party model capabilities.

astra-6.text:
The starting point is understanding what success looks like for the customer. “Make the model better” isn’t specific enough. You need to get down to a concrete task: What information does Asimov have, what actions can it take, and what outcome would make the customer say, “Yes, that’s what I needed”? Then you can turn that into an evaluation.

The tricky part is making sure the evaluation captures the actual need. A response can look good and still fail to accomplish the task. So you want to measure the outcome, and then inspect the trajectory to understand where things went wrong. Did it misunderstand the request? Did it lack some context? Did it take the wrong action?

That gives you a feedback loop: take a customer failure, reproduce it in an evaluation, use that to guide an improvement, and check that the improvement generalizes beyond that one example. The evaluations become a concrete way of translating what customers care about into what you’re trying to improve.

r001.rationale: It says to understand customer success and translate needs into evaluations, but does not frame this as the AI-era counterpart of startup customer discovery.

r002.rationale: It starts from the customer's concrete task and desired outcome, then asks what information and actions the system needs and turns that into an evaluation.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss restricting changes to product features or agent design, or dependence on third-party model capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
We try to start with the actual task the customer wants to get done. What does success look like? What information does Asimov have access to? What constraints does it need to respect? You want to turn those questions into something you can test, rather than just asking whether an answer looks good.

Then you run the system, look at where it fails, and make those failures part of the evaluation. Did it misunderstand the objective? Did it miss information? Did it take the wrong action? That distinction matters because those problems require different fixes.

The loop is customer task, evaluation, failure analysis, improvement—and then checking that the improvement actually helps on new tasks. The evaluation has to stay connected to what the customer values, or you can end up improving a score without making the product more useful.

r001.rationale: The response starts from customer tasks and success criteria, but does not frame evaluation development as the AI-era counterpart of startup customer discovery.

r002.rationale: It works from the customer’s task, desired success, available information, and constraints to define tests, then uses failures to guide system improvement.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss limiting changes to product features or agent design, or dependence on third-party model capabilities.
